patients.summary: Marine mechanic with transfusion-acquired hepatitis C who joins in 2018, decompensates with hepatocellular carcinoma in 2021, has a bridge resection and a liver transplant in 2022, then a perforated duodenal ulcer, tacrolimus nephrotoxicity, two ICU stays in 2025 (septic shock with central diabetes insipidus, then ARDS), and necrotizing fasciitis of the left leg in 2026 after the practice last saw him.

Records release form emailed for his prior office.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
53M new to me. Previous PCP retired; records requested.

Hep C: picked up years ago, he thinks it came from blood he got in the 80s. Genotype 1a per what he remembers from old paperwork. Never treated. He was told at some point he could get the newer pills but never followed up on it. No jaundice, no swelling of the belly or legs, no confusion, no GI bleeding.

Reflux: on and off for 10+ years, uses calcium carbonate chews when it acts up, maybe twice a week. Had an ulcer a long time ago, can't recall the year or what was done, no surgery.

Alcohol: drank heavily for many years. Stopped in 2016 on his own, nothing since. Father drank and died with cirrhosis, which he says is part of why he quit.

PMH: as above. PSH: none. Meds: calcium carbonate 500 mg chew PRN. Allergies: none to medications.
FH: father alcohol use disorder with cirrhosis; paternal uncle had liver cancer; mother type 2 diabetes.
SH: self-employed, repairs outboard and inboard marine engines out of his own shop. Never smoked. No drugs. Single.

ROS: negative except heartburn as above.

Exam: well appearing. No scleral icterus. Heart RRR, no murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, nontender, no organomegaly palpable, no fluid wave. No spider angiomas, no palmar erythema. No edema. Neuro grossly normal, no asterixis.

A/P
1. Chronic hepatitis C, untreated: CMP, CBC, INR, viral load today.
2. GERD with remote PUD: stable on PRN calcium carbonate.
3. Alcohol use disorder in remission since 2016: commended.
4. Health maintenance: HIV screen with labs. Tdap today. Lipids. Will talk colon screening at his physical.
RTC 6 months.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Robert, your labs are back. Your liver enzymes are mildly up, which is typical with hepatitis C. Your liver's protein production, clotting test and blood counts are normal. Hepatitis C virus level is 1.45 million. HIV test negative. Cholesterol and kidney function fine. We will keep watching these. Flu shots arrive next month, stop in any morning for one.

documents.title: Flu Vaccine

documents.body: Walk-in for flu vaccine. No prior reactions, feels well. Quadrivalent flu given L deltoid, tolerated. VIS given.

Physical in September.

A/P: healthy-appearing 54M with chronic untreated hep C, GERD, alcohol use disorder in remission. Labs ordered. Follow up spring.

orders.reason: jaundice, weight loss, chronic hepatitis C

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: tired, poor appetite, weight loss, yellow eyes.

HPI: 56M with untreated chronic hep C. About 3 months of steadily worse fatigue and less appetite; fills up after a few bites. Weight down from 88 to 81 kg without trying. Vague ache across the upper belly, queasy on and off. Eyes yellow and urine tea-colored for ~2 wks. Denies fever, vomiting blood, black stools, travel. No alcohol since 2016, confirms again today. No new meds or supplements.

Exam: tired-appearing. Scleral icterus. Abdomen distended, mildly tender in the upper abdomen, hard to assess the liver edge with the distension. No asterixis. No edema.

A/P: jaundice and weight loss in a man with long-standing hep C. Concerned for advanced liver disease, need to exclude a liver mass.
- CMP, CBC, INR today.
- Urgent GI referral; called their office, they can see him 6/9.
- No alcohol, no NSAIDs, acetaminophen no more than 2 g a day if needed.
- ER precautions reviewed.

documents.title: Lab results and GI appointment
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Called pt per PCP. Bilirubin 3.6, albumin 2.9, INR 1.5, platelets 121, liver enzymes up modestly. PCP wants him to keep the GI consult 6/9 at 10:30; he has the address. Reviewed reasons to go to the ED. Pt verbalized understanding, will bring a list of questions.

conditions.label: Decompensated cirrhosis of liver
conditions.note: Hepatitis C with prior alcohol use; jaundice and ascites

medications.sig: Take 1 tablet by mouth every morning

reports.text: Complete abdominal ultrasound. Liver is coarse in echotexture with a nodular surface, consistent with cirrhosis. A large irregular heterogeneous solid mass is seen in the right hepatic lobe. Main portal vein patent with hepatopetal flow. Moderate ascites. Gallbladder without stones or wall thickening. Common bile duct not dilated. Kidneys normal in size without hydronephrosis. Abdominal aorta of normal caliber.
reports.conclusion: Cirrhotic liver with a large irregular right hepatic lobe mass. Moderate ascites. Multiphase CT or MRI recommended.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Consultation
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY AND HEPATOLOGY GROUP
Date of service: 06/09/2021
Thank you for referring Mr. Nowak, a 56-year-old marine mechanic with chronic hepatitis C, genotype 1a, from transfusions in the 1980s, never treated.

He has three months of worsening tiredness, poor appetite, early fullness, intermittent nausea and an indistinct abdominal ache, with weight loss. Over the past couple of weeks his eyes have turned yellow and his urine dark. No fever, hematemesis or travel. He drank heavily for years and stopped in 2016. He has never received hepatitis A or B vaccine.

Meds: calcium carbonate as needed. Allergies: NKDA.
Family: father with alcohol-related cirrhosis; a paternal uncle with liver cancer; mother with type 2 diabetes.

Exam: chronically ill-appearing man with scleral icterus and mild temporal and shoulder-girdle wasting. The abdomen is distended with a fluid wave; a firm nodular liver edge is felt below the right costal margin.

Data: your labs from 5/26 show mildly raised AST and ALT, a raised alkaline phosphatase and a prolonged INR. Alpha-fetoprotein drawn today is 212 ng/mL. Ultrasound here today shows a cirrhotic liver with a large, irregular mass in the right lobe and ascites.

Impression:
1. Decompensated cirrhosis from hepatitis C and prior alcohol, with jaundice and ascites.
2. Right hepatic lobe mass with raised AFP, highly concerning for hepatocellular carcinoma.

Plan:
- Multiphase CT abdomen within two weeks.
- Spironolactone 100 mg daily with furosemide 40 mg daily; 2 g sodium diet; BMP in 2 to 3 weeks through your office.
- Referral to transplant hepatology.
- Please vaccinate against hepatitis A and B.
- Continued abstinence; no NSAIDs.
We will see him back after imaging.

conditions.label: Hepatocellular carcinoma
conditions.note: 4.0 cm right lobe, LI-RADS 5; transplant candidate

reports.study: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast
reports.text: Multiphase liver protocol: noncontrast, late arterial, portal venous and delayed phases through the abdomen, portal venous phase through the pelvis. The liver is small and nodular in contour, consistent with cirrhosis. In the right hepatic lobe there is a 4.0 cm lesion with arterial phase hyperenhancement, nonperipheral washout on portal venous and delayed phases, and an enhancing capsule. No other liver lesion. Portal and hepatic veins are patent without tumor thrombus. Moderate ascites. No adenopathy. Kidneys, adrenals and pancreas unremarkable. No bony lesion. Bowel unremarkable. Lung bases clear.
reports.conclusion: 4.0 cm right hepatic lobe observation, LI-RADS 5, definite hepatocellular carcinoma. Cirrhosis with moderate ascites. No portal vein thrombosis. No extrahepatic disease.

documents.title: CT Abdomen and Pelvis, Liver Protocol
documents.author: radiology
documents.body: Outside imaging center report received by fax. Ordered by gastroenterology, copy to PCP. Findings: 4.0 cm right lobe lesion meeting LI-RADS 5 criteria in a cirrhotic liver; moderate ascites; portal vein patent; no spread outside the liver.

documents.title: CT results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Robert, I saw the CT report. GI called you yesterday, I know, but I wanted to check in myself. The spot in the liver is a liver cancer, and the scan shows it has not spread outside the liver. The transplant team referral is the right next step and GI has already sent it. Please come see me in a couple of weeks: we need a blood test on the water pills and we can start your hepatitis vaccines. Call me any time with questions.

documents.title: RE: CT results
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Thanks for reaching out. Kind of numb about it still. I'll set up the appointment. Peeing a lot on the new pills but the belly feels a little better.

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Here after GI and CT. Knows the diagnosis: HCC 4 cm in the R lobe, cirrhosis with ascites. Transplant hepatology intake call scheduled for August. Taking spironolactone 100 and furosemide 40 every morning. Abdomen less tight, weight down about 1.5 kg since GI. Eyes still a bit yellow. Some lightheadedness standing up quickly, no falls. Working half days.
O: vitals as charted. Mild icterus. Abdomen distended, soft, shifting dullness. No edema. No asterixis.
A/P:
1. HCC, R lobe, LI-RADS 5: per GI and transplant hepatology.
2. Decompensated cirrhosis with ascites on diuretics: BMP today.
3. Never vaccinated for hep A/B: hep A #1 and hep B #1 today; hep B #2 in 1 month, both completed in January. PCV20 today.
4. Low sodium diet reviewed; handout.
Follow-up 3 months, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Kidney function, sodium and potassium all fine on the water pills. No changes. Nurse visit in about 4 weeks for the second hepatitis B shot.

documents.title: Hepatitis B Vaccine #2
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Hep B dose 2 given L deltoid. No reaction to dose 1. Next doses (hep A #2, hep B #3) due early January; reminder set.

documents.title: Transplant Hepatology Evaluation
documents.author: transplant hepatology
documents.body:
REGIONAL LIVER TRANSPLANT CENTER, HEPATOLOGY
Date of visit: 08/11/2021
Mr. Nowak was seen for liver transplant evaluation on referral from his gastroenterologist.
Diagnoses: decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C genotype 1a and prior alcohol use (abstinent since 2016), with ascites on spironolactone and furosemide; a single 4.0 cm LI-RADS 5 hepatocellular carcinoma in the right lobe without vascular invasion or spread.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Assessment: he is a candidate for liver transplantation, and his tumor burden falls within standard transplant criteria. His sobriety history is documented and was reviewed with our social work team.
Plan: complete the candidate evaluation (cardiac testing here, dental clearance). Please arrange a colonoscopy, which is required before listing. We note hepatitis A and B vaccination has begun in your office; please complete both series. Our surgical colleagues will review whether a bridging treatment of the tumor is appropriate while he awaits a graft.
We will keep you informed.

documents.title: Colonoscopy Report
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE ENDOSCOPY CENTER
Procedure date: 09/22/2021
Indication: colon cancer screening, required for liver transplant listing; no prior colonoscopy.
Sedation: monitored anesthesia care. Prep: good, mucosa well seen throughout.
Findings: scope passed to the cecum, appendiceal orifice photographed, terminal ileum briefly entered and normal. No polyps, masses or bleeding. Retroflexion in the rectum unremarkable.
Impression: normal colonoscopy.
Recommendation: repeat screening in 10 years. Allergies: NKDA.

documents.title: Follow-up Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: Colonoscopy done 9/22, normal. Transplant center finishing his evaluation; cardiac testing there next month. Yellow tint fading. Belly has stayed about the same size on the diuretics. Appetite a bit better. Still sober. Back to most of his usual work, avoiding heavy lifting.
O: vitals as charted. Faint icterus. Abdomen mildly distended, nontender, shifting dullness present. No edema. No asterixis.
A/P:
- HCC R lobe, awaiting transplant center plan.
- Decompensated cirrhosis: labs today (CMP, CBC, INR). Diuretics unchanged.
- Vaccines: flu and first recombinant zoster dose today, before any immunosuppression. Hep A #2 / hep B #3 / zoster #2 in January.
RTC 3 months.

reports.text: Liver contour is nodular with coarse echotexture. Right hepatic lobe solid mass measuring 4 cm. Main portal vein patent with hepatopetal flow; no portal vein thrombus. Large volume ascites. Gallbladder unremarkable. No biliary dilatation. Kidneys normal in size without hydronephrosis.
reports.conclusion: Nodular cirrhotic liver with a 4 cm right lobe mass. No portal vein thrombosis. Large volume ascites; site marked for paracentesis.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Follow-up
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY AND HEPATOLOGY GROUP
Date of service: 12/13/2021
Mr. Nowak, 56, with hepatitis C cirrhosis and a 4 cm right lobe HCC under transplant evaluation, comes back with two months of the abdomen steadily enlarging and uncomfortable despite spironolactone 100 mg and furosemide 40 mg. He has had no alcohol, no fever and no change in bowel habit.
Allergies: NKDA. Meds: spironolactone, furosemide, calcium carbonate as needed.
Exam: tense distended abdomen with a fluid wave and shifting dullness. No jaundice. No lower extremity edema.
Ultrasound today: nodular liver, 4 cm right lobe mass, portal vein patent.
Diagnostic paracentesis performed under ultrasound guidance, left lower quadrant, without complication. Fluid grossly bloody. Ascitic hematocrit 10%. SAAG 1.1 g/dL. Ascitic total protein 3.2 g/dL. Cytology sent and pending.
Blood: hemoglobin 12.5, platelets 110,000, INR 1.2, AFP 400 ng/mL.
Assessment: refractory-trending ascites with portal hypertension; bloody fluid in the setting of HCC raises concern for tumor-related bleeding or seeding, and the cytology is important before listing. Thrombocytopenia from portal hypertension. AFP rising.
Plan: await cytology; we have discussed the case with the transplant team, who will see him early January about bridging therapy. Continue diuretics.

results.text: Negative for malignant cells. Blood and reactive mesothelial cells.

documents.title: Peritoneal Fluid Cytology
documents.author: pathology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE PATHOLOGY
Specimen: peritoneal fluid, diagnostic paracentesis 12/13/2021.
Diagnosis: negative for malignant cells. Background blood with reactive mesothelial cells and scattered lymphocytes.
Copy to referring gastroenterologist and PCP.

documents.title: Vaccine Series Completion
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Here to finish his series before surgery later this month. Hep A #2 R deltoid, hep B #3 L deltoid, recombinant zoster #2 L deltoid (separate site). Sore arm and tired for a day after the first zoster dose, nothing else. Observed 15 min, fine. Hep A, hep B and zoster series now complete; copy faxed to the transplant coordinator per their request.

reports.text: Specimen: liver, right lobe, partial hepatectomy. Gross: a portion of nodular liver containing a well-circumscribed tan-yellow tumor, 4.0 cm in greatest dimension. Microscopic: hepatocellular carcinoma. Background liver: established cirrhosis.
reports.conclusion: Hepatocellular carcinoma, 4.0 cm, in a cirrhotic liver.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: transplant surgery
documents.body:
REGIONAL LIVER TRANSPLANT CENTER, SURGICAL SERVICE
Admitted: 01/26/2022  Discharged: 02/04/2022
Diagnosis: hepatocellular carcinoma, right lobe, in hepatitis C cirrhosis; on the transplant waiting list.
Procedure 01/26: exploratory laparotomy and partial hepatectomy of the right-lobe tumor, as a bridge while he awaits a donor liver. Tumor removed intact.
Course: extubated in the OR. Two days in the surgical ICU for monitoring, then the floor. Diuretics resumed day 4. Ambulating, tolerating a regular low-sodium diet at discharge.
Pathology: hepatocellular carcinoma, 4.0 cm, in a cirrhotic liver.
Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge meds: spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, calcium carbonate as needed.
Follow-up: surgical clinic in 2 weeks; ultrasound in 6 weeks; hepatology in 4 months. PCP visit in 2 weeks.

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Post-Hospital Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
S: 13 days out from laparotomy and partial hepatectomy at the transplant center. Pain now just soreness at the incision, most days needs nothing for it. Eating ok, bowels moving. Walking a mile a day. Surgeon saw him Monday, staples out. Still on spironolactone/furosemide.
O: afebrile, vitals as charted. Mild icterus no longer seen. Right subcostal incision healed, no redness or drainage. Abdomen soft, slight distension, no tenderness.
A/P:
- HCC s/p resection 1/26; path reviewed. Remains listed for transplant.
- Cirrhosis: BMP today on diuretics.
- No lifting over 10 lb for 6 weeks per surgery, so no engine work until March. He is not thrilled.

reports.text: Status post partial right hepatectomy. Expected postsurgical appearance of the resection margin without collection. Liver nodular and coarse. No focal liver mass. Portal vein patent with hepatopetal flow. No ascites. Gallbladder unremarkable. No biliary dilatation. Spleen and kidneys unremarkable.
reports.conclusion: Postsurgical change after partial right hepatectomy. No new liver mass. No ascites.

documents.title: Gastroenterology Follow-up
documents.author: gastroenterology
documents.body:
OUTSIDE GASTROENTEROLOGY AND HEPATOLOGY GROUP
Date of service: 06/06/2022
Interval: partial right hepatectomy for HCC in January at the transplant center; he remains on the waiting list. The March ultrasound after surgery showed no new mass and no ascites.
Over about two months his belly has been swelling again with some discomfort. He denies any alcohol, fever or bowel change.
Meds: spironolactone 100 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, calcium carbonate as needed. Allergies: NKDA.
Exam: ascites with a fluid wave. Several spider angiomas over the upper chest and shoulders. Healed right subcostal incision.
Labs today: platelets 110,000, INR 1.3, albumin 3.2, total bilirubin 2.1, AST 80, ALT 75, alkaline phosphatase 120. AFP 150 ng/mL, down from 400 before resection.
Assessment: decompensated hepatitis C cirrhosis with recurrent ascites after resection; AFP falling but not normal.
Plan: continue diuretics and 2 g sodium restriction; MELD labs every month per the transplant center; we can arrange a large-volume paracentesis if he becomes uncomfortable. Transplant hepatology to repeat cross-sectional imaging.

documents.title: Liver Transplant Discharge Summary
documents.author: transplant surgery
documents.body:
REGIONAL LIVER TRANSPLANT CENTER
Admitted: 09/19/2022  Discharged: 09/30/2022
Indication: decompensated cirrhosis from chronic hepatitis C (genotype 1a) and prior alcohol use, with hepatocellular carcinoma treated by partial right hepatectomy in January 2022.
Procedure 09/19: orthotopic deceased-donor liver transplantation. Uneventful anastomoses. Extubated postoperative day 1.
Course: graft function improved steadily with falling bilirubin and INR. Graft ultrasound on day 1 and day 5 showed patent vessels. Ascites resolved; diuretics stopped. Transferred from the ICU on day 3. Tacrolimus titrated to target trough.
Allergies: no known drug allergies.
Discharge medications:
- tacrolimus 2 mg by mouth twice daily
- mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg by mouth twice daily
- prednisone 5 mg by mouth daily
- trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 160/800 mg by mouth daily (Pneumocystis prophylaxis)
- calcium carbonate 500 mg as needed for dyspepsia
Stopped: spironolactone, furosemide.
Follow-up: transplant clinic twice weekly for the first month with labs, including tacrolimus troughs; then tapering visits. PCP within 2 to 3 weeks. No live vaccines. Inactivated influenza vaccine may be given after the first month.

1. Liver transplant status: immunosuppression per transplant center. Problem list updated: cirrhosis, portal hypertension and low platelets resolved with the new liver; HCC moved to history. Platelets normal today.
2. Chronic hepatitis C: remains on the list.
3. Labs today as a courtesy for transplant clinic, results faxed there.
4. Vaccines: inactivated flu and updated COVID in November once past the first month. No live vaccines ever going forward, reviewed.

procedures.procedure: Patch repair of perforated duodenal ulcer

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL HOSPITAL EMERGENCY DEPT
Visit 12/03/2022, arrived 16:45 by private car.
CC: abdominal pain, sudden, 2 hours.
HPI: 57-year-old man about 10 weeks after liver transplant. Abrupt severe pain across the whole abdomen that started while watching TV and has not let up; nothing makes it better or worse. For about a week, burning in the pit of the stomach after eating, which he treated with over-the-counter antacids now and then; did not call anyone. Takes prednisone and other transplant medicines. Never smoker, no alcohol.
Allergies: NKDA.
Vitals: T 38.2 C, BP 96/60, HR 112.
Exam: lying very still, sweaty. Abdomen distended, tender everywhere with guarding and marked rebound. No bowel sounds.
Upright CXR: free air under the diaphragm.
Impression: perforated viscus, likely peptic, in an immunosuppressed patient. Fluids, IV antibiotics, IV PPI. Transplant team and general surgery at bedside; to the OR.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Date of operation: 12/03/2022
Preoperative diagnosis: pneumoperitoneum. Postoperative diagnosis: perforated anterior duodenal ulcer.
Procedure: exploratory laparotomy, omental (Graham) patch repair of perforated duodenal ulcer, washout.
Findings: a small perforation of the anterior wall of the first part of the duodenum with bilious contamination of the upper abdomen. Liver graft appeared healthy. No other perforation.
The omental pedicle was secured over the defect with interrupted sutures; leak test negative. Abdomen irrigated. Fascia closed. EBL minimal. Patient to the surgical ICU in stable condition.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Admitted: 12/03/2022  Discharged: 12/10/2022
Diagnosis: perforated duodenal ulcer, s/p Graham patch repair 12/03. Background: liver transplant 09/2022 on tacrolimus, mycophenolate, prednisone.
Course: one night in the surgical ICU, then the floor. IV antibiotics completed. Diet advanced from day 4. Tacrolimus continued with levels checked by the transplant team throughout. Wound healing well.
Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: pantoprazole 40 mg twice daily for 8 weeks (new); tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily; mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily; prednisone 5 mg daily; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS daily.
Instructions: avoid NSAIDs. Surgical clinic 2 weeks. PCP 1 to 2 weeks.

documents.title: Hospital Follow-up

documents.title: Nephrology Consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
COMMUNITY HOSPITAL, NEPHROLOGY CONSULT SERVICE (ED)
Date: 02/15/2024
Asked by the ED to see this 58-year-old man, liver transplant 09/2022 on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone, with a remote perforated duodenal ulcer repair. Two days of feeling unwell with headache and passing less urine. He says he takes his tacrolimus exactly as prescribed, 2 mg twice daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
BP 162/98. Mild edema of both lower legs. Otherwise unremarkable.
Creatinine 2.8 mg/dL (his baseline 1.0). BUN 44. Potassium 5.2. Tacrolimus level 25 ng/mL against a target of 5 to 15. Urinalysis: specific gravity 1.030, protein negative, no cells.
Impression: acute kidney injury from calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, with a supratherapeutic tacrolimus level. Bland, concentrated urine fits a hemodynamic, vasoconstrictive effect.
Recommendations: hold tacrolimus and recheck the level daily; gentle IV fluids; avoid nephrotoxins and contrast; resume per transplant hepatology once the level is back in range. Discussed with the transplant center.

conditions.note: Inadequately controlled during septic shock; responded to vasopressin

documents.title: ICU and Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: pulmonary and critical care
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER, MEDICAL ICU
Admitted: 03/07/2025  Discharged: 03/19/2025
Principal diagnosis: septic shock secondary to pneumonia.
Secondary: central diabetes insipidus, inadequately controlled during the acute illness.
Background: 59-year-old man with chronic hepatitis C, prior hepatocellular carcinoma, liver transplant 09/2022 on tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone; earlier tacrolimus nephrotoxicity (02/2024) and perforated duodenal ulcer repair (12/2022).
Course: admitted to the ICU from the ED with pneumonia and shock. He received high-volume IV fluids and broad-spectrum IV antibiotics. Over the first two days his pressure stayed low despite resuscitation and he became increasingly drowsy and confused, so norepinephrine was begun. Urine output remained over 4 liters a day even while he was hypotensive. Vasopressin was added; within about 12 hours nursing recorded a clear fall in urine output and he was noticeably less thirsty, consistent with central diabetes insipidus. He was fed enterally for several days with electrolytes replaced as needed. Exam during the stay showed no edema or JVD, unremarkable heart and lung sounds and no focal neurological deficit.
Pressors were weaned off by day 6, mental status cleared, and he finished his antibiotic course on the ward. At discharge urine output and serum sodium were normal without desmopressin.
Immunosuppression: managed with the transplant center throughout; discharged on his usual doses.
Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS daily, calcium carbonate as needed.
Follow-up: PCP within 1 to 2 weeks; transplant clinic 2 weeks. Return for fever, cough, breathlessness, confusion, or heavy urination with thirst.

documents.title: ICU and Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: pulmonary and critical care
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER, MEDICAL ICU
Admitted: 04/04/2025  Discharged home: 04/29/2025
Diagnoses: septic shock secondary to pneumonia (readmission four weeks after the March ICU stay); acute respiratory distress syndrome with refractory hypoxemia.
Background: 59-year-old liver transplant recipient (09/2022) on tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil and prednisone, with central diabetes insipidus identified during the March admission.
Course: returned with pneumonia and shock and needed fluid resuscitation, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, vasopressors and intubation with mechanical ventilation on arrival to the ICU.
ICU day 3 (04/06): oxygenation had deteriorated over 24 hours with steadily rising inspired oxygen requirements. He was febrile and tachypneic, with diffuse crackles through both lungs. Arterial gases showed hypoxemia that did not correct with supplemental oxygen. Chest film: bilateral patchy opacities, no cardiomegaly. Echocardiogram: preserved LV systolic function and no significant valve disease, arguing against a cardiac cause. Diagnosis: ARDS with refractory hypoxemia.
Lung-protective ventilation was used. Because he is immunosuppressed, bronchoscopy with BAL was done on 04/07 to look for an opportunistic infection: bacterial culture no growth, Pneumocystis PCR not detected, galactomannan negative. Antibiotics were completed for bacterial pneumonia.
Oxygenation improved over the following week. Extubated 04/15. Stepped down to the ward 04/18 and worked with physical therapy until discharge. Room air at discharge.
Immunosuppression adjusted day to day with the transplant team and resumed at usual doses before discharge.
Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS daily, calcium carbonate as needed.
Follow-up: PCP 2 to 3 weeks; transplant clinic 1 to 2 weeks.

Second ICU admission in two months: 4/4-4/29, recurrent septic shock from pneumonia, intubated, ARDS with refractory hypoxemia on 4/6. BAL negative for opportunistic organisms. Extubated 4/15. Discharge summary reviewed in full.
S: Home 2.5 weeks. Weak legs, walks the driveway and back twice a day, using a cane outside. Breathing better each week, winded on stairs. No fever, minimal cough. Eating three meals, weight down to 75 kg from 83 last fall. Urinating normally, no excess thirst at night. Saw transplant clinic last week; no med changes. Not back at work and not sure when.
O: SpO2 94% on room air at rest. Vitals otherwise as charted. Thin, tired but in no distress. Lungs: clear to auscultation. Heart regular. Abdomen soft. No edema. Gait slow but steady.
A/P:
1. ARDS after septic shock from pneumonia: recovering, on room air. Resolved off the active list; recovery will take months.
2. Central diabetes insipidus: no polyuria; sodium today.
3. Calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity: creatinine today.
4. Liver transplant on tacrolimus/mycophenolate/prednisone: per transplant center.
5. Deconditioning: home walking plan reviewed, increase gradually.
CMP and CBC today. Return in about 2 months, sooner if needed.

events.reason: left lower leg pain and swelling after a laceration

documents.title: Emergency Department Record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER EMERGENCY DEPT
Seen 06/04/2026 at 19:50.
CC: left lower leg pain and swelling for 24 hours.
HPI: 61-year-old liver transplant recipient. Yesterday he nicked the front of his left shin while cleaning his boat; within a few hours it began to hurt badly and swell, and it has worsened since. History of chronic hepatitis C and past alcohol misuse.
Meds: tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, prednisone, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, calcium carbonate as needed. Allergies: NKDA.
Vitals: T 38.9 C, HR 112, BP 90/60.
Exam: left lower leg red, swollen and very tender, with several blood-filled bullae. Small laceration on the anterior shin.
Labs: WBC 18,000, hemoglobin 13.2, platelets 230,000, sodium 135, potassium 4.5, creatinine 1.2, AST 80, ALT 72, total bilirubin 2.1, PT 16 seconds, INR 1.4.
Impression: necrotizing soft tissue infection of the left leg with sepsis in an immunosuppressed patient.
Plan: IV fluids, broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, blood cultures; emergency general surgery consult; transplant team notified. To the OR tonight.

documents.title: Operative Report
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
Date of operation: 06/04/2026
Preoperative and postoperative diagnosis: necrotizing fasciitis, left lower extremity.
Procedure: extensive surgical debridement of skin, subcutaneous tissue and fascia of the left lower leg.
Findings: grayish, nonviable fascia with thin dishwater fluid, separating easily from the underlying muscle along the anterior and lateral leg. Muscle viable. All nonviable tissue excised back to bleeding, healthy tissue. Tissue sent for culture and pathology.
Wound packed and dressed.

documents.title: Hospital Discharge Summary
documents.author: general surgery
documents.body:
REGIONAL MEDICAL CENTER
Admitted: 06/04/2026  Discharged: 06/18/2026
Diagnosis: necrotizing fasciitis, left lower extremity, after a minor laceration.
Procedures: emergency extensive surgical debridement of the left lower leg on 06/04; wound managed with packing and dressing changes.
Course: monitored in the surgical ICU for the first 48 hours; blood pressure recovered with fluids. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics, narrowed and completed in hospital in consultation with infectious disease. Immunosuppression continued in coordination with the transplant center. Fever resolved, white count normalized, and the wound bed is healthy and granulating.
Allergies: NKDA.
Discharge medications: unchanged from admission (tacrolimus 2 mg twice daily, mycophenolate mofetil 750 mg twice daily, prednisone 5 mg daily, trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole DS daily, calcium carbonate as needed).
Discharged home with visiting nurse wound care and dressing changes three times weekly.
Follow-up: surgical clinic in 1 week; transplant clinic in 2 weeks; PCP at his convenience.

documents.title: Out of the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Wanted you to know I was in the hospital two weeks for a bad leg infection after I cut my shin on the boat. They operated on it. Home now, nurse comes three times a week for the dressing. Surgeon sees me Friday. Do you need me to come in?

documents.title: RE: Out of the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Robert, thank you for telling me, and I'm sorry you went through that. I have the hospital records. For now the surgeons and the wound nurse are the right people for the leg. Once you're getting around, call the front desk and we'll find a time to catch up; it has been a while. Any fever, spreading redness or feeling faint, go straight to the ER.
